label: Evaluating Geometric Estimators
notes: This chapter, printed pages 132 to 150, asks how good an estimated transformation really is. We separate two questions: how well the estimate fits the noisy data, and how close it sits to the truth. The whole lecture builds tools to measure error and propagate uncertainty.

label: Residual versus Estimation Error
notes: Stress that these two errors answer different questions. Residual compares the estimate against noisy measurements; estimation error compares it against the noise-free truth. Four correspondences interpolate perfectly, so residual is zero yet the transfer is noisy. Adding points raises the residual but constrains the truth, lowering estimation error.

label: Measurement and Model Manifold
notes: Set up the geometric picture. Measurements live in a high-dimensional space; the model manifold is every measurement reachable by some parameter vector. Maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise finds the nearest manifold point. This nearest-point view is what turns estimation into orthogonal projection on the following slide.

label: Tangent-Plane Projection Identity
notes: Explain the linearization. Replacing the curved manifold by its tangent plane makes maximum likelihood an orthogonal projection, so the measured-to-true vector splits into estimated-to-true plus measured-to-estimated legs that are perpendicular. Pythagoras then gives the squared-error identity the notebook verifies to machine precision, the backbone of the bounds.

label: Performance Bounds
notes: Walk through the bound formulas. With N measurements and d essential parameters, residual scales with the parameters projected away and estimation with the parameters kept. For one-image homography noise, N equals two n and d equals eight; the two-image case also estimates point positions, so d grows. Residual rises while estimation falls.

label: Covariance by Forward Propagation
notes: Introduce first-order propagation. A function f carries an input covariance to an output covariance through the Jacobian sandwich J Sigma J transpose. This forward rule is the workhorse: feed it the covariance of measurements or of homography entries and it returns the covariance of any derived quantity, such as a transferred point.

label: Backward Propagation to Parameters
notes: Contrast backward propagation. To get the covariance of estimated parameters we invert the information matrix J transpose Sigma inverse J. Because a homography is homogeneous, it has a scale null direction, so the information matrix is rank deficient and we take a pseudo-inverse. The notebook confirms the information rank is eight.

label: Confidence Ellipses
notes: Make covariance visual. The eigenvectors of a two-by-two covariance give the ellipse axes and its eigenvalues set their lengths; scaling by the chi-square quantile fixes the confidence level. Mahalanobis distance is the natural metric, and its square follows a chi-square law, so a chosen probability picks the ellipse radius directly.

label: Transfer Covariance Under a Homography
notes: Connect propagation to point transfer. The transfer Jacobian maps homography-entry covariance to a point covariance, J h Sigma h J h transpose. On the unit-circle correspondences the ellipses stay tight inside the support but balloon outside it; the radial uncertainty grows like root one plus r to the fourth, exposing extrapolation risk.

label: Monte Carlo Covariance
notes: Present Monte Carlo as the empirical audit. We perturb the data many times, re-estimate, and collect a cloud of outputs whose sample covariance we fit with an ellipse. It needs no Jacobian and so validates the linear theory, exposing bias, variance, and degeneracy that small-noise formulas might silently miss.

label: Configuration Hides Degeneracy
notes: Drive home the warning from the Monte Carlo run. Well-spread and nearly collinear layouts gave almost identical training residuals, yet the collinear probe-transfer covariance was tens of thousands of times larger. A small reprojection residual does not certify a reliable transformation; the point configuration governs covariance far more than the residual.

label: Evaluation Workflow Recap
notes: Close with the workflow. Always report residual and estimation error, propagate covariance to the quantity you will actually use, compare against the lower bound, and confirm with Monte Carlo across noise levels and configurations. Evaluation is geometric: residual, parameter covariance, and extrapolation each measure something different.
